newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. takes special security precautions.
newsitem.headline: U.N. takes special security precautions.

text.p: The United Nations on Tuesday took special security precautions after discovering four letter bombs addressed to the U.N. bureau of an Arabic-language newspaper.

Hundreds of thousands of letters and parcels were screened over the last 24 hours in seach of the bombs, which U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said "have a similar X-Ray imprint to a musical greeting card." In addition journalists who work in the building and messengers were given security briefings.

The four bombs, with Alexandria, Egypt, postmarks, were sent to the U.N. bureau of London-based Al-Hayat newspaper and discovered on Monday and on Tuesday night. They did not explode but were safely defused, some with water cannons.

They were part of an apparent campaign against the paper owned by a member of Saudi Arabia's royal family. Similar devices were mailed this month to the paper's bureaus in Riyadh, London and Washington.
Hours before the U.N. bombs were discovered a letter bomb exploded on Monday at Al-Hayat's London headquarters, wounding two security guards. There were no injuries in any of the other locations.

No one has claimed responsibility although the attacks and the plastic explosives used have prompted suspicion that Arab militants are behind the campaign. Al-Hayat editors have speculated that the newspaper may have made enemies by its even-handed coverage of the Middle East.

The United Nations normally receives about 20,000 pieces of mail daily but with the accumulation from the weekend security personnel are sifting through about 80,000 letters and parcels, Eckhard said.

In an unprecedented move, members of the U.N. press corps, who have offices in the building, were briefed by U.N. security staff and New York City bomb squad members on recognising potential explosives and what to do if they came across a suspicious object. Cameras and tape recorders were excluded from the secret session.
Eckhard later told his regular daily briefing: "If you find a suspicious item, call security right away. Don't open it, don't handle it unecessarily and let them come up and take a look at it."
The U.N. complex on Manhattan's East River functioned normally and tourists, albeit fewer than normal, continued to arrive.

James Kallstron of the Federal Bureau of Investigation said all the cards mailed to al-Hayat around the world were similar, in greeting-card-sized white envelopes. He said they all bore a Dec. 21 postmark from Alexandria, even though they arrived over a period of two weeks, and a joint New York police-FBI anti-terrorist task force was working closely with authorities in Egypt.

In Cairo, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak expressed doubt the bombs came from Egypt, saying it was "easy to imitate the stamps, to imitate everything (and) post them here and there." He complained that his government had not received an original of the envelopes, although 11 days had passed since the first letter bomb was detected in Washington.

Five letter bombs were also found this month at Levenworth Federal Prison in Kansas and a sixth was found at the Leavenworth post office. Mohammad Salameh, a militant Moslem, is serving a life sentence there for the bombing attack on the World Trade Centre in 1993 and two other men have been jailed at Leavenworth for their part in a conspiracy to blow up the United Nations and other buildings in New York.
On Jan. 11, five letter bombs were received at the Al-Hayat bureau in Washington. No one was injured.

At the United Nations the first bomb was found on Monday morning 15 minutes before it was to have been delivered to AL-Hayat. Its correspondent, Raghida Dergham, had alerted U.N. security to check her mail because of the London incident.
